Reference · design

Architecture

One process, one file, six sockets. How a measurement travels from a frame to a committed row, how a wide query avoids scanning millions of points, and what bounds memory while all of it runs at once.

Process one, asyncio, SQLite in the same loop Storage monthly partitions, WITHOUT ROWID Write batched, one transaction per burst Read rollup for finished hours, raw for the edges Bounds every queue and cache has a stated limit

The shape of it

One process, one SQLite file, six ports. A measurement arrives on a socket, is committed in a batch, and is readable and streamable within milliseconds. This page explains how, and why each piece is the way it is.

Words used on this page

Ingress — the receive path: socket to validated rows.
Persister — the task that commits batches.
Partition — one monthly table, measurements_YYYY_MM.
Series — one metric with one exact tag set.
Rollup — the hourly summary, rollup_hourly.
Watermark — the next hour the rollup will process.
Broker — the socket that answers queries.
Fan-out hub — the in-process path to WebSocket subscribers.
Bounded queue — a limit with real backpressure behind it.
HWM — a socket's high-water mark.
WAL — SQLite's write-ahead log, which makes commits crash-atomic.

One process, and why

SQLite allows exactly one writer. Almost every design decision below follows from taking that seriously rather than working around it.

The message layer, the query facade and the HTTP gateway all run in one process, in one asyncio event loop, against one engine. That removes every question about serialising across a process boundary, and it means a query can read the live engine directly instead of asking another process for the answer and getting a second copy of the truth back.

The schema

Three tables, plus the schema version table that tracks migrations. That is the whole thing.

-- one row per (metric, tags) — the series identity
CREATE TABLE series (
    series_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    metric     TEXT NOT NULL,
    tags       TEXT,     -- JSON text, and CHECK (json_valid(tags))

    CONSTRAINT ck_tags_json CHECK (tags IS NULL OR json_valid(tags))
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_series_metric_tags ON series(metric, tags);

-- one per month, created on demand
CREATE TABLE measurements_2026_09 (
    series_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    timestamp_ns INTEGER NOT NULL,
    value        REAL    NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (series_id, timestamp_ns)
) WITHOUT ROWID;
CREATE INDEX ix_measurements_2026_09_ts ON measurements_2026_09 (timestamp_ns);

-- the hourly summary the query fast path reads
CREATE TABLE rollup_hourly (
    series_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    hour_start_ns INTEGER NOT NULL,
    count INTEGER NOT NULL,
    sum   REAL    NOT NULL,
    min   REAL    NOT NULL,
    max   REAL    NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (series_id, hour_start_ns)
) WITHOUT ROWID;

-- how far the rollup has advanced
CREATE TABLE rollup_meta (k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, v INTEGER NOT NULL);
Why the tags are JSON in one column

A tag set is a dimension of arbitrary size. Storing it as JSON in one TEXT column means a series is one row, the uniqueness constraint is (metric, tags) on a real index, and there is no join to resolve before a write. The cost is that you cannot query by tag on the SQL path — which is the same trade the high-cardinality warning on Ingestion exists to discourage.

The CHECK constraint is the backstop: even if validation were bypassed entirely, a tag set that is not valid JSON cannot be stored.

Why WITHOUT ROWID

The measurement table's primary key is its data. Storing it that way removes the separate rowid index entirely — one B-tree instead of two, and no indirection to follow. Because the key starts with series_id, all of one series' points are physically adjacent, so a time-range read on one series is a sequential scan of a contiguous range.

The secondary index on timestamp_ns alone covers the other access pattern: cross-series time windows, and retention.

Why monthly partitions

Retention is the reason. Dropping data that is a month old is DROP TABLE — instant, and it returns the pages to the file — rather than a mass DELETE that rewrites indexes and leaves free pages scattered. It also keeps each table small enough to stay in the page cache, so a query against last month touches a small file rather than a huge one.

The write path

Four stages, and the order is the design.

  1. ReceiveThe PULL socket is drained in batches with NOBLOCK. Each frame is parsed and validated. Invalid frames are counted and dropped; they never reach the queue.
  2. EnqueueThe batch is put on a queue bounded by a counting semaphore with pending_max credits. When the credits run out the receive loop suspends, and the socket's HWM takes over.
  3. PersistA dedicated task takes each batch and commits it in one BEGIN IMMEDIATE, off the event loop in a worker thread. Rows are grouped by partition, so a burst spanning a month boundary still commits atomically.
  4. PublishOnly after the commit succeeds, the batch is republished to the stream. One task per burst, not one per point.
Why the receive loop never awaits the commit

Because the alternative caps ingest at the disk's write rate. Measured on 2026-09-09: awaiting commits inline held ingest to roughly 1,650 points/second while the pump was offering 10,000. Decoupling the receive from the commit is what closes that gap.

The danger of decoupling is an unbounded buffer, and that is what pending_max prevents. The bound is explicit, the backpressure behind it is real, and no data is dropped to keep up. The full ladder is on Ingestion.

Why BEGIN IMMEDIATE and not BEGIN

A plain BEGIN is deferred: it takes a read snapshot, and the later upgrade from a read lock to a write lock returns SQLITE_BUSY immediately under WAL, because the busy handler is not consulted for a lock upgrade. BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock up front, so busy_timeout applies and writers queue properly.

What happens when a batch fails

The whole batch is dropped and its size added to dropped. The worker survives. A PULL socket has no acknowledgements — the producer has already sent and moved on — so the choice is between dropping and stalling. Dropping visibly beats stalling invisibly, and dropped is on the admin socket and the dashboard for exactly this reason.

The accounting identity holds: every accepted point lands in exactly one of persisted, dropped or invalid. The test suite asserts it.

The query path

Three routes, chosen by what the question needs.

Query shapeRouteWhy
Whole-window aggregate, five of the ten functions, window inside rolled hoursrollup a few dozen summary rows instead of millions
Bucketed, and the function is one of avg/sum/min/max/count SQL SQLite groups per bucket, so Python never sees a raw row
Anything else — raw, or median/p95/p99/first/last, or gap fillingraw scan those functions cannot be derived from count/sum/min/max

What makes a query eligible

All four must hold, or the raw path is used:

  • the aggregation is one of avg, sum, min, max, count;
  • any interval is a whole number of hours;
  • the window ends at or before the rollup watermark;
  • the window spans at least two hours — narrower than that and there is nothing to accelerate.
Why the last rule is a feature

For a window under two hours the raw path is genuinely faster: it reads one partition with one index, while the rollup path would read the summary table, read two raw edges, and then merge three sets of partials. More work, not less. The eligibility test exists so the fast path is used where it wins and skipped where it does not.

Why publish is not the read path

Every finished hour is summarised once the clock passes it — and then waits the client clock-skew window before doing so. The reason is a correctness invariant: a write arriving late must never land in an hour that has already been summarised, or it would be invisible to every rollup-served query. Since late writes are bounded by reject_client_timestamp_skew_s, the rollup waits exactly that long. The current hour is therefore always read live, which is why the results are never stale.

When a write lands in a rolled hour anyway

The skew guard makes a late write rare, not impossible. A producer with a drifted clock, a replayed batch, or a deliberate historical load can still write a point whose hour has already been summarised.

That point used to be stored, reported as written, and then omitted from every rollup-served answer — silently, because the rollup only ever moved forward and never revisited the hour. The write looked successful and the aggregate was wrong.

So the write path rewinds the watermark. When the oldest timestamp in a drained batch falls behind it, rewind_watermark() pulls the watermark back to that hour inside the same transaction as the data, so the watermark and the data it describes move together and the next pass re-aggregates. Re-aggregation uses INSERT OR REPLACE, so replaying the same backfill twice is idempotent. The cost is one single-row lookup on a one-row table, once per batch.

The rewind then exposed a second defect in the settle step. Taking min(completed, current) cannot distinguish a rewind that landed during the roll from one that already existed beforehand, so a single backfill pinned the watermark to that hour permanently: the log reported the advanced value, the table kept the old one, and every later pass re-scanned the same range. The settle step now compares against the watermark read before rolling, so a rewind invalidates the pass only when the value moved backwards since the pass began.

Background tasks

Four, each with an interval. None of them runs on the event loop, but not all of them avoid the write path: rollup and retention write through the single writer transaction, so a pass serialises against ingestion for as long as it holds the lock. Backup and maintenance use a pooled connection.

TaskEveryDoesIf disabled
Rolluprollup.interval, 5m Summarises newly-finished hours into rollup_hourly, then advances the watermark. queries stay correct, but wide ones scan raw rows
Retentionretention.check_interval, 1h Drops whole partitions whose month is entirely past the TTL, rollup rows included. the file grows without bound
Maintenanceanalyze_interval, 1h ANALYZE, to keep query-planner statistics current as the data changes. the planner's estimates drift and query plans worsen
Backupbackup.interval, 24h A VACUUM INTO snapshot into backup.path. no automatic snapshots; use sqtseries backup

Each runs its first pass immediately on boot — so a fresh instance gets a partition, a snapshot and a catch-up rollup without waiting an interval — and then sleeps. Every blocking pass runs in a worker thread, so a large catch-up on an old database never stalls the event loop or the service's start-up.

There is also a WAL checkpoint manager on a 60-second timer, which is what stops the WAL file growing without limit. It counts how often a checkpoint was blocked by a long reader, because a rising checkpoint_busy_runs means something is holding a read snapshot open — see Backup.

Concurrency

One writer, several readers, and a pool that cannot deadlock.

ResourceHow it is managed
Writerone persistent connection behind a lock. A handle that fails is quarantined, closed, and lazily replaced — so one bad transaction can never wedge every future write.
Readersa LIFO pool of 4. LIFO, not FIFO, because the most recently returned connection has the warmest page cache; FIFO would hand out the coldest first.
Over-subscriptionwhen every reader is checked out, a further checkout gets a small transient handle instead of waiting. Bounded waiting is deadlock prevention: nothing ever waits indefinitely, so there is no circular wait.
Off-loop workan 8-thread executor for every blocking job — queries, HTTP writes, dashboard snapshots. Unbounded, the default executor spawns a thread per concurrent slow job, which multiplied under a query storm.
Event loopnever blocked by SQLite. Every query and write runs in a thread, so streaming and health checks stay responsive under load.
One measured decision worth knowing

The pump serves one request per step rather than bursting through everything queued. Burst-serving makes tight clients finish faster, which raises per-second allocation churn until the allocator holds gigabytes — measured at 1.3 GB after 300 s. One recv per step keeps churn at a rate a single worker can absorb, while ordinary clients still see handler-time latency because the answer comes from the SQL path.

This is a case where the obvious optimisation was measurably worse, and the comment in the source says so with the number attached.

Every bound, and every counter

The single most consistent thing about the design: nothing is unbounded, and nothing fails silently.

BoundDefaultWhen it fillsCounted as
Ingest HWM101,000 framessenders block — (that is the backpressure)
Pending batches100the receive loop suspends backpressured
Query max_rows10,000 the query is refused, not truncated MAX_ROWS_EXCEEDED
Query max_inflight64 total requests stay in the socket pipequeries_shed
Query timeout30 sthe handler is abandoned QUERY_TIMEOUT / 504

Cache weight200,000 rowsleast-recently-used evicted—

HTTP per minute600 per peer429 RATE_LIMITED
Dashboard backlog500 framesthe oldest is dropped—
Shutdown flush60 sthe persister is cancelled loudlyan error log
Graceful HTTP stop5 sstragglers are cancelled—
The query cap is one global pool, not 64 per client

max_inflight bounds the broker's dispatch tasks, and there is exactly one such set for the whole process (len(broker._router_tasks) >= max_inflight in messaging/broker.py). It is not a per-connection quota, and it is not per client. Eight clients do not get 512 dispatches; they share 64.

This matters when you load-test it, because the mistake is silent in the harness and looks like a slow server. A client that permits itself 64 unanswered requests while running eight of them lets 512 requests pile up against a broker servicing 64, so the broker sheds most of them — and the honest-looking report then says the generator was too slow. Read queries_shed before blaming the server: a non-zero value means requests were refused at the door, not that they were slow inside.

Why the counters matter more than the bounds

A bound tells you the system will not grow without limit. The counter tells you whether the bound is being hit. Every one of them is readable from the admin socket, the HTTP API and the dashboard, so a bound being reached is an observation rather than a mystery.

The two you should alert on are dropped and invalid. A non-zero value means data is not being stored, for a reason that is visible.

How latency is measured, and how to not fool yourself

Every latency number for this project comes from scripts/stress_percentiles.py. It has two load models, and the difference between them is larger than most of the numbers it reports.

Closed loop: what a client sees

The default model. Each client sends a request and waits for the reply before sending the next. This is what a ZeroMQ REQ socket physically is — it cannot send again before it receives — so it is not a shortcut, it is the protocol.

Its failure mode is coordinated omission. When the server stalls, the clients stall with it, so the offered load drops at exactly the moment the system is slowest, and the recorded tail comes out optimistic. The result answers one question honestly: at saturation with N clients, what is the response time? It is not an arrival-rate measurement.

Open loop: what an arrival stream sees

With --model open the harness issues requests on a fixed schedule regardless of whether replies have come back, and measures each one from the time it was due rather than the time it was sent. The queueing delay a stall causes is therefore counted instead of hidden. Two socket-level details make this work, and both are easy to get wrong:

  • A REQ socket is lockstep, so the open-loop client uses DEALER, which pipelines, against the broker's ROUTER.
  • The broker replies [identity, "", payload]. REQ strips those two frames for you; DEALER does not, so the client must take the last frame of recv_multipart(). Calling recv_json() on a DEALER tries to parse the raw identity bytes and raises JSONDecodeError.

Two figures are recorded for every request, and the gap between them is the measurement:

FieldMeasured fromReads as
zmq_querythe actual send service time — what one client experienced
zmq_query_cothe scheduled fire time arrival-rate behaviour, corrected for coordinated omission
Measured, same machine, 8 clients, 2,000 pts/s ingest alongside

Unsaturated at a 250 ops/s offered rate, the two agree — which is the check that the correction is not simply adding a fudge factor:

zmq_query p50 30.59 ms / p99 138.27 ms  ·  zmq_query_co p50 30.73 ms / p99 138.40 ms

Saturated, the same correction separates them by 6.8× at p50 — the queueing delay that closed-loop measurement hides:

zmq_query p50 1,434 ms / p99 2,591 ms  ·  zmq_query_co p50 9,780 ms / p99 29,957 ms

Three numbers that decide whether a run means anything

scripts/stress_percentiles.py --model open reports these so a broken generator cannot quietly report a healthy rate. Check all three before quoting anything:

  • sent_ops — frames the broker actually accepted. If this is 0, the generator never fired and the run describes nothing. A pacer that sleeps without sending still reports a perfect achieved rate.
  • zmq_query n — replies matched. This must equal sent_ops. A shortfall means requests went unanswered.
  • client_shed — how often the generator hit its own in-flight cap. Non-zero means the offered rate was not achieved, so the run does not certify that rate. It is a limit on the claim, not a fault in the server.

Because of that last one, a saturated open-loop run publishes a corrected latency but not a certified arrival rate: the harness pushes what it can and the report says so.

# closed loop (default) — saturation with N clients
scripts/run-stress-rig.sh --duration 300 --rate 2000 --clients 8 --tag baseline

# open loop — a paced arrival stream, corrected for coordinated omission
scripts/run-stress-rig.sh --duration 300 --rate 2000 --clients 8 \
    --model open --query-rate 250 --tag arrival

# --max-inflight is the cross-client total, mirroring the broker's global cap.
# The default 64 splits to 8 per client at 8 clients; setting it per-client
# instead lets 8x the broker's budget pile up and the broker sheds.

Run these through scripts/run-stress-rig.sh, which wraps the whole process tree in scripts/mem-guard.sh so a runaway run cannot take the machine down. Full tables and the accounting identities are on Benchmarks; the coordinated-omission literature is Gil Tene, How NOT to Measure Latency, and Friedrich et al., Coordinated Omission in NoSQL Database Benchmarking (BTW 2017).

SQLite settings, and the ones that look wrong

Every new connection gets the same set. Full list with rationale on Configuration; the two worth explaining are here.

SettingValueWhy
journal_modeWAL Readers do not block the writer, which is what makes a single-writer design workable from several threads at once.
synchronousNORMAL With a WAL, NORMAL is durable across an application crash — which is the failure that actually happens. Only an OS-level crash can lose the most recent commit, and that trade buys a large write rate.
cache_size-8000 per connection 8 MB, not the 64 MB the setting nominally implies. A large cache on a shared handle makes glibc arena allocation balloon, because free() returns memory to its allocating thread's arena — so total resident memory climbs with threads times working set. Measured at 10k pts/s: 60–100 MB of anonymous arena per handle.
wal_autocheckpoint0 readers, 10,000 writer Reader connections never trigger a checkpoint, so they cannot contend with the writer. The writer checkpoints every ~80 MB, ten times fewer fsync spikes than the 1,000-page default.
busy_timeout5000 ms So a contended writer waits rather than failing.
temp_storeMEMORY Spills for sorts and grouping go to memory, not a temp file.
page_size8192, fresh files only SQLite cannot change it after creation, and it must be set before WAL, so the bootstrap connection skips WAL entirely.
auto_vacuumINCREMENTAL, fresh files only Same constraint. Lets PRAGMA incremental_vacuum return space in slices instead of a full rewrite.

Why checkpoints run on the writer connection

The wal_autocheckpoint row above sets readers to 0 and the writer to 10,000, which settles automatic contention. It does nothing about manual contention, and that gap is why this subsection exists.

SQLite documents a corruption bug — the WAL-reset bug, in section 11 of the WAL documentation — which fires when two connections on the same file "attempt to write or checkpoint at the same instant". One checkpoint resets the WAL while the other connection commits. The second checkpoint does not notice the reset, leaves the wal-index claiming frames it never copied, and a later checkpoint skips them. Part of a committed transaction never reaches the database file, and the file goes corrupt.

The background checkpoint manager used to reach SQLite through connect(), which returns a pooled reader, while writes ran on a separate writer connection. Four readers and a writer on one file, with a timer firing every 60 seconds, is exactly the documented trigger. checkpoint() now takes the writer handle under the writer lock instead, so write and checkpoint land on one connection and cannot interleave on any SQLite version. A checkpoint briefly blocks writers, which costs nothing: SQLite allows only one writer at a time anyway.

Running an unpatched SQLite is not an exposure

The bug is present from 3.7.0 through 3.51.2. It is fixed in 3.51.3 and later, with backports in 3.50.7 and 3.44.6.

sqtseries does not depend on yours being patched. The serialization above removes the precondition, so the buggy state is unreachable regardless of version. Upgrade for defence in depth, not to close a hole.

If you do check sqlite3.sqlite_version, compare within the series: 3.51.1 sorts above 3.50.7 but is older than the fix, so a naive comparison reports a false pass. There is also rarely a packaged upgrade to point at — Ubuntu 26.04 ships 3.46.1 and has not backported it, and the pysqlite3-binary wheel bundles 3.51.1, which is also unfixed. Moving past it means building SQLite from source.

Durability and recovery

At start-up

  1. MigrateApply pending schema migrations idempotently, then ensure the current month's partition exists.
  2. Check integrityPRAGMA quick_check, non-strict, so a damaged file is reported rather than silently repaired.
  3. Recover the WALReplay any frames that were committed but not yet merged. This is what makes a hard kill survivable.
  4. Bind the socketsAll six, with the five fixed ports reserved before the ingest detector runs — which is what stops the detector handing out 12506 and then failing to bind the stats publisher.
  5. Start the tasks, write the runtime fileOnly after every socket has bound is ANALYZE run, so a failed boot in a restart loop does not hammer the planner statistics on every attempt.
The runtime file is the last thing removed

On clean shutdown, removing runtime.json is the final step. A restart script that waits for it knows the process has truly exited — which kill -0 alone cannot tell you, because a zombie that has not been reaped still answers to signal 0. A failed second start never deletes the healthy instance's runtime file, so a rejected start cannot take the running service's state with it.

At shutdown

Ordered, and the order is the point: stop the tasks, drain the socket before closing it, flush the persister, drain the brokers and the gateway, await in-flight publishes, then PRAGMA optimize and a checkpoint. That last one is TRUNCATE only when the WAL is 4 MB or smaller, and PASSIVE above it: the timer-driven pass is always PASSIVE, and a large one-pass reset is the shape that has been observed to cross-link b-tree pages. The full sequence is on Systemd.

Why one process

SQLite allows one writer. Putting the message layer, the query facade and the HTTP gateway in the same process removes every inter-process serialisation question, and lets a query run against the live engine without a second copy of the truth. The cost is that the service is a single point of failure — which the systemd unit and the retention and backup tasks are there to cover.

The write path never waits for the disk

The receive loop parses frames and hands each batch to a dedicated persister through a bounded queue. Awaiting the commit inline would cap ingest at the disk's write rate; decoupling it is what lets a sustained pump persist far more than that. The bound is the queue, so the decoupling cannot become an unbounded buffer.

Why the hourly summary is exact

The rollup stores count, sum, min and max per series per finished hour. Every average is then a division of two stored columns, so a rollup-served answer is not an estimate of an average — it is the same average, computed from sufficient statistics. This is the reason the fast path can be trusted for alerting.

Partitions, not one growing table

A monthly table per month means retention is a DROP TABLE rather than a mass DELETE, and each table stays small enough for the page cache. The cost is a table per month and a partition-name lookup on the write path, both cheap.

Every bound is stated, and every drop is counted

Pending batches, fan-out queue bytes, cache entries, cache weight, in-flight queries, WebSocket connections, HTTP requests per minute. Each has a limit in the settings, and each drop or shed shows up in a counter. A bounded system that loses something silently is worse than an unbounded one that is honest.

sqtseries — how the pieces fit, and why.

Every default on these pages is the default in the code, checked against sqtseries --help, the live settings loader and the running service by scripts/docs-build/verify_docs.py. The wire format is the same on every transport: ZMQ PULL, ROUTER, REQ, XPUB, HTTP and WebSocket.
